scams.name: Charleston 'Oldest Scam in the Book' — Palmetto Rose & Street Vendor Hustle
scams.description:
Travelers call Charleston's long-running "palmetto rose" hustle the oldest scam in the book. Individuals at City Market and along Meeting Street approach tourists, quickly weave a palmetto-frond rose (it takes ten seconds), hand it to a spouse or older traveler "as a gift," then demand $10 to $30 in cash "for the art." The traveler feels obligated to pay because the rose is already in their hand. Variants include fake "charity" buckets rattled at tourists with sob-story cards; an aggressive "fortune teller" who grabs your hand before reading, then demands $40 or more; and a fake "photographer" who snaps an unsolicited picture of you on Meeting Street, then charges $15 to $25 "for the memory."

For older travelers in Charleston's historic core, the defensive playbook is straightforward. Keep your hands in your pockets or holding a bag strap near City Market, and refuse all unsolicited "gifts." If a palmetto rose is placed in your hand, return it immediately without entering into any negotiation. Do not respond to "fortune teller" or "photographer" approaches — give a firm "no thank you" and keep walking. Genuine palmetto roses are available at reputable Gullah artisan stalls inside City Market with posted prices of $3 to $10, so pay for a displayed product rather than an unsolicited "gift." For aggressive demands, the Charleston Police Department non-emergency line is 843-743-7200.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets near City Market and refuse all unsolicited "gifts." Return a palmetto rose immediately if it is placed in your hand. Give a firm "no thank you" to fortune tellers and unsolicited photographers. Buy genuine palmetto roses at Gullah artisan stalls with posted $3 to $10 prices. Report aggressive demands to the Charleston Police Department at 843-743-7200.
scams.location: Charleston City Market, Meeting Street, Market Street intersection, Waterfront Park, Rainbow Row perimeter
scams.tldr: Charleston's "oldest scam": someone weaves a palmetto-frond rose in ten seconds, presses it into your hand "as a gift," then demands $10 to $30 "for the art" because you're already holding it. Fake charity buckets, hand-grabbing fortune tellers, and unsolicited "photographers" work the same blocks around City Market and Meeting Street.

scams.name: Charleston Restaurant Deceptive Menu, Fake Local Shrimp & Tipping Overcharge
scams.description:
Charleston had a restaurant-deception scandal in 2025: travelers report that 90% of Charleston restaurants were found to be deceiving customers, and a local shrimp scandal named 25 restaurants. SC DNR and SCELP tested shrimp at 44 restaurants advertising "local shrimp" and found 40 (91%) were actually imported farm-raised shrimp from Asia priced at a local-shrimp premium — $28 to $38 for "local" when the shrimp cost the restaurant $4 a pound wholesale imported. The scam takes several forms: a menu listing "local shrimp and grits" at $28 or more when the shrimp is imported; "wild-caught local" claims without verification; an auto-gratuity of 20% to 22% added to parties of two without disclosure; a viral Charleston restaurant gratuity overcharge of 523%; and a "service charge" of 3% to 5% that is not gratuity.

For older travelers dining in Charleston, the protective playbook is clear. For genuine local shrimp, use the SC Shrimpers Association "Certified SC" list at certifiedsc.com — Magnolia's, Husk, FIG, and Hominy Grill are verified. Ask the server directly, "Is this shrimp wild-caught local or imported farm-raised?" — honest restaurants will tell you. Always check the bill for auto-gratuity, service charge, and tip-on-tax before signing. At Shem Creek, Red's Ice House and Shem Creek Bar & Grill are verified local. For budget Low Country eats, Hyman's Seafood (touristy but honestly priced), Brown Dog Deli, and Callie's Hot Little Biscuit are fair. Report fraudulent menu claims to SC DNR at scdnr.gov/shrimpscandal.
scams.avoidance: Use the "Certified SC" list at certifiedsc.com for verified local shrimp. Ask the server directly, "Is this wild-caught local or imported?" Check the bill for auto-gratuity, service charge, and tip-on-tax before signing. Magnolia's, Husk, FIG, and Hominy Grill are verified local. Report menu-claim fraud to SC DNR at scdnr.gov/shrimpscandal.
scams.location: Meeting Street tourist restaurants, Market Street waterfront dining, King Street tourist strip, Shem Creek seafood venues
scams.tldr: A 2025 Charleston scandal found that 40 of 44 restaurants advertising "local shrimp" (91%) were actually serving imported farm-raised shrimp at a $28 to $38 local premium. Tourist restaurants also pad bills with undisclosed auto-gratuity, hidden service charges, and tip-on-tax — including one viral 523% tip overcharge.

scams.name: Charleston Horse Carriage Tour & Walking Tour Tourist Trap
scams.description:
Charleston carriage tours run $30 to $50 per person for historic-district tours via Palmetto Carriage Works, Old South Carriage Company, and Classic Carriage Works — legitimate operators whose routes are randomized by a city medallion lottery. There is an active local debate over carriage tours, and several scams and concerns recur. Hotel concierges mark up tours to $65 to $95 per person versus $30 to $50 booked direct. "Private charter" upsells run $300 to $500 for what are shared 16-passenger carriages. Route "upgrades" at $20 or more have no effect, since routes are randomized by the city lottery. There are also summer animal-welfare concerns: Charleston suspends carriage tours above 95°F under a city ordinance, but some operators continue anyway. And walking-tour touts charge $45 for what costs $25 booked direct.

For older travelers in Charleston, the practical rules are simple. Book direct with Palmetto Carriage Works (palmettocarriage.com, $34), Old South Carriage Company ($38), or Classic Carriage Works ($33). Ride early in the morning (9 to 11 a.m.) or late in the afternoon (after 4 p.m.) in summer. On days forecast above 95°F, confirm the tour will actually run, since the city ordinance suspends tours in extreme heat. Shared tours are $30 to $50, so private charters at $300 or more are mostly markup. For walking tours, Charleston Footprints ($25) and Bulldog Tours ($30) are reputable direct bookings — skip curb touts at $45 or more. The historic district is highly walkable for older travelers, with two- to three-hour tours covering the Battery, Rainbow Row, the Dock Street Theatre, and St. Philip's Church.
scams.avoidance: Book carriage tours direct: Palmetto Carriage Works ($34), Old South ($38), or Classic Carriage Works ($33). Ride early morning or late afternoon in summer. Refuse tours offered on days above 95°F, when a city ordinance suspends them. Use Charleston Footprints ($25) or Bulldog Tours ($30) for walking tours. Pay by credit card for chargeback leverage.
scams.location: Charleston City Market carriage stand, Broad Street carriage waiting zone, Meeting Street tour-kiosk strip
scams.tldr: Charleston carriage tours cost $30 to $50 booked direct, but hotel concierges mark them up to $65 to $95, "private charters" run $300 to $500 for shared 16-passenger carriages, and route "upgrades" do nothing since routes are set by a city lottery. Some operators also run tours above 95°F despite a city ordinance suspending them.

scams.name: Charleston 'Great Vacations LLC' & Meeting Street Timeshare Hustle
scams.description:
Charleston has a specific timeshare-hustle operation at 180 Meeting Street, the Great Vacations LLC Travel Club. The pattern works like this: a promoter on the street or in a hotel lobby offers a "free Charleston tour," a "$100 dinner voucher," or a "free harbor cruise" in exchange for attending a "90-minute presentation." The presentation actually runs three to five hours, with aggressive pushing of $10,000 to $40,000 "travel club" or "vacation ownership" purchases. The targets are older travelers perceived as having disposable retirement funds, and the pitch leans on "today only" pricing pressure and "7-day rescission" claims that are often misrepresented. Variants include a "Vacation Club" membership at $8,000 to $20,000 with opaque annual fees, and "exit" companies charging $5,000 to $15,000 upfront to "cancel an existing timeshare" — many of which are themselves scams.

For older travelers in Charleston, the defensive posture is firm. Never accept "free gift" offers that require attending a "presentation" — the time cost and pressure tactics are a net negative even with free gifts. If you do attend, bring a printed "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. South Carolina offers a five-day right of rescission for timeshare contracts, so cancel within five days if you signed under pressure. For rescission help, use the SC Attorney General's Consumer Protection division (scconsumer.gov), not "exit" companies charging $5,000 or more. Report Great Vacations LLC or similar operations to the SC Attorney General and the Charleston Better Business Bureau.
scams.avoidance: Never accept "free gift" offers that require attending a presentation. If you attend, bring an "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. Use South Carolina's five-day right of rescission if you signed under pressure. Report to the SC Attorney General's Consumer Protection division at scconsumer.gov. Avoid "exit" companies charging $5,000 or more — use the state Attorney General instead.
scams.location: Meeting Street timeshare sales offices (180 Meeting St historically), Isle of Palms / Kiawah resort presentation venues, Charleston hotel lobbies
scams.tldr: At 180 Meeting Street, Great Vacations LLC offers a "free harbor cruise" or "$100 dinner voucher" for a "90-minute presentation" that actually runs three to five hours of high-pressure pitching toward $10,000 to $40,000 "travel club" purchases, targeting retirees. "Exit" companies promising to cancel timeshares for $5,000-plus are often scams too.

scams.name: Charleston CHS Airport Rideshare & Taxi Overcharge
scams.description:
Charleston International Airport (CHS) is 12 miles from downtown Charleston, and legitimate fares are: Uber or Lyft, $22 to $35 depending on surge (pickup at Garage Level 3); a licensed taxi with the meter running, $30 to $42; and the CARTA airport express bus, $3.50 (on a limited schedule). The market is rideshare-dominant, but several scams recur. Drivers solicit at baggage claim offering a "flat $55 to downtown" for what is a $22 to $35 Uber. "Limo" or "black car" touts quote $100 or more for standard trips. Uber and Lyft drivers sometimes demand a cash tip beyond the app total at drop-off. Weekend Uber surge pricing can hit $45 to $60 or more when a licensed taxi is $30 to $42, so check both before ordering. And "shuttle" touts offer a "downtown shuttle" at $80 when Uber is $25.

For older travelers arriving at CHS, the clean route is straightforward. Take Uber or Lyft from the designated pickup at Garage Level 3 with a fare screenshot ($22 to $35 to downtown). Use a licensed taxi at the taxi stand with the meter running ($30 to $42 to downtown). The CARTA airport express at $3.50 is the cheapest option but is schedule-limited, so check carta.com. During peak Uber surge (Friday evening, Sunday afternoon), compare the taxi-stand rate — the taxi is often cheaper at those times. Avoid "flat rate $55" drivers at baggage claim, who are unlicensed. And never pay a cash tip beyond the Uber app total, since app-entered tips are already processed.
scams.avoidance: Take Uber or Lyft from the designated pickup at CHS Garage Level 3 with a fare screenshot. Use a licensed taxi with the meter running ($30 to $42 to downtown). The CARTA airport express is $3.50 (check carta.com for the schedule). Compare Uber surge against the taxi-stand rate at peak times. Pay tips through the app only, and refuse cash-tip demands after the ride.
scams.location: Charleston International Airport (CHS), rideshare pickup zone (CHS garage level 3), licensed taxi queue, baggage claim solicitors
scams.tldr: From Charleston airport (12 miles out), a legitimate Uber or Lyft runs $22 to $35, a metered taxi $30 to $42, and the CARTA bus $3.50. Watch for baggage-claim drivers pushing a "flat $55," "black car" touts quoting $100-plus, $80 "shuttle" offers, and drivers demanding cash tips beyond the app total.

scams.name: Charleston Restaurant Tip-on-Tax & Auto-Gratuity Tipping Overcharge
scams.description:
Beyond the local-shrimp scandal, Charleston tourist restaurants run standard tipping-overcharge patterns, including a viral 2025 case in which a restaurant charged a 523% tip through a credit-card terminal misentry. Common variants include "tip on post-tax total," where some terminals default to calculating suggested tips on the post-tax amount, inflating the "standard 20%" by 7% to 10%; pre-filled "suggested tip" lines at 22%, 25%, and 28% rather than 15%, 18%, and 20%; an auto-gratuity of 20% added to parties of two to four without clear menu disclosure; a "service charge" of 3% to 5% that is not gratuity, with the server still expecting a tip on top; and handwritten bills where the total line is left blank for the server to fill in after you leave.

For older travelers dining in Charleston, the protective rules are simple. Always check the bill for "gratuity," "service charge," or any auto-added amount before signing. Calculate your intended tip on the pre-tax subtotal, which is standard practice. Cross out the "suggested tip" lines and write your chosen amount in the "additional tip" field. Always fill in the "TOTAL" line yourself — never leave it blank. Keep the merchant receipt and check your credit-card statement within 48 hours, and dispute any overcharge through your credit card immediately with a photo of your signed receipt. At reputable venues such as Husk, FIG, Magnolia's, Slightly North of Broad, and Hominy Grill, tipping practices are standard and transparent.
scams.avoidance: Check the bill for auto-gratuity and service charges before signing. Calculate your tip on the pre-tax subtotal, not the post-tax total. Always fill in the "TOTAL" line yourself — never leave it blank. Keep the merchant receipt and check your credit-card statement within 48 hours. Dispute overcharges through your credit card with a photo of the signed receipt.
scams.location: Tourist-facing Meeting Street, Market Street, and King Street restaurants; Shem Creek seafood venues
scams.tldr: Charleston tourist restaurants inflate tips by calculating them on the post-tax total, pre-filling "suggested" lines at 22% to 28%, adding undisclosed auto-gratuity to small parties, tacking on non-gratuity "service charges," and leaving the total line blank to fill in after you go — one viral 2025 case charged a 523% tip.
